consensus_summary: “Stranger” broadly signifies an outsider or alien, with major applications to those outside God’s covenant, vulnerable foreigners to be welcomed, and believers who live as pilgrims in the world.
book_summary: “Stranger” is defined specifically through theological citizenship: one outside God’s covenant commonwealth who may be drawn into it, after which the believer becomes a stranger to the world.
consensus_core_identification: An outsider or alien, especially either someone outside the covenant community or a believer whose true home is not the present world.
book_core_identification: A non-citizen of God’s commonwealth who is incorporated into it and consequently becomes alien to the world.
boundary_disagreement: The book restricts the symbol to covenantal and spiritual citizenship. It excludes strangers understood merely as literal foreigners, vulnerable guests, or unknown persons, while combining two recognized consensus cases—covenant alienation and Christian pilgrim status—into a sequential pattern.
material_contradiction: None. Both stages of the book’s definition are recognizable consensus meanings, though the consensus does not require them to form one sequence or exhaust the term’s significance.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus category of the stranger as an outsider but specifies the relevant boundary as membership in God’s commonwealth and, after incorporation, alienation from the world. This is a material narrowing rather than a new or contradictory referent.
strongest_objection: Ephesians 2:12 and 2:19 strongly support being outside the covenant and then admitted as a fellow citizen, but they do not themselves support the added claim that the admitted person is thereby made a stranger to the world; nor do they establish the entry’s full exclusion of social and hospitality senses.
